We take straight, isolated microtubule stretches from SMLM fields in the ShareLoc repository ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ) , cut each at a point, and rotate it rigidly, with no rescaling or resampling, so that the cut lands on a common vertex. A cross joins two stretches (four arms, crossing angle drawn from 30 ∘ 30^{\circ} to 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} ); a T-junction joins a stretch and a half-stretch (three arms, 35 ∘ 35^{\circ} to 145 ∘ 145^{\circ} ). Each has a control in which one arm of a straight pair is turned by 25 ∘ 25^{\circ} to 45 ∘ 45^{\circ} . A measured empty disk from the same field supplies background, and all arms are at least 30 ∘ 30^{\circ} apart. Every localization is measured, with its own blinking and precision; only the placement is synthetic. The window center is offset from the vertex by up to 50 nm, and the methods see localizations only. From each junction we draw n ∈ { 25 , 50 , 100 , 200 , 400 , 800 } n\in\{25,50,100,200,400,800\} localizations. Three studies had written protocols, frozen before any evaluation fit: data, construction, methods, settings, endpoints and analysis. Each has 120 junctions. The cross-laboratory study uses 27 fields of COS-7, REF52 and U2OS cells from two laboratories, two dyes and two camera types; the U-373 study 28 fields of U-373 MG cells; the unused acquisitions study 22 fields from 34 acquisitions that no earlier analysis had opened, with reference directions taken from localizations of the same stretches that are not in the fitted subsample. No field was used for development. Exact recovery means the correct count and every arm within 10 ∘ 10^{\circ} of its reference. The main comparator is a Hessian ridge detector: it renders the localizations at 10 nm, smooths at 50 nm, keeps the strongest 70% of ridge pixels between 0.35 ​ R 0.35R and R R , and reads the arms from peaks of the strength-weighted orientation histogram. Its settings were tuned on development fields.

Because the fit estimates the blur of every window while the detector smooths at one width, we also ran the same detector with automatic scale selection at every pixel ( Lindeberg, 1998 ) , choosing among eleven scales from 15 to 100 nm by a normalized ridge strength. Its settings were calibrated on 240 junctions of an earlier study that shares no field with these three, and it was then run once on every stored window; since the three studies had been analysed before, this comparison is retrospective (Appendix B.4 ). Four more detectors, Steger’s detector in its ImageJ implementation ( Steger, 1998 ) , a line fit, angular histograms and skeletonization, are reported in Appendix C ; the likelihood fit beats each of them in each study. Points beyond the window can.

The continuation check keeps a candidate arm added by a larger count only if its sector holds more localizations than the neighbouring sectors in both of two rings between R R and 2 ​ R 2R (a one-sided binomial test with a family level of 0.05 0.05 ). Part B of the unused-acquisition study tests it on 60 junctions whose second filament was thinned so that each of its arms holds 2 to 8% of the window, and on the same 60 geometries unthinned. Both detectors miss these arms almost always, and the agreement rule removes arms that the BIC had right. The continuation check restores them: it adds 50.3 50.3 points [ 37.6 , 64.5 ] [37.6,64.5] of count accuracy at 400 and 800 localizations, raising the correct count at 800 from 0.26 to 0.79, and it adds no extra arm at 100, 400 or 800 localizations (Figure 10 ). Photon arrivals are independent, as in Theorem 5 . After a first study with generic starts failed its prespecified criteria, we fixed a new protocol and applied the fit to 30 new sources taken in a fixed random order from the public archive, with directions from calibration alone, photons of 0.5 to 8 keV within 1000 detector pixels ( 492 ′′ 492^{\prime\prime} ) of the source image, and n ∈ { 100,200,400,800 } n\in\{100,200,400,800\} with three draws each (Appendix B.1 ).

The calibrated directions agree with a map fitted to all photons of each observation within 0.0016 ∘ 0.0016^{\circ} . The likelihood runs with instrument floors (arms 4 ∘ 4^{\circ} apart, arm shares at least 0.004 0.004 ) and chooses one or two blur components by BIC. The ray model is an approximation here: each arm starts some distance from the source image, its intensity follows the source spectrum, and the line-spread function has wings. When all four arms are found within 10 ∘ 10^{\circ} (18, 24, 36 and 38 of 90 draws at 100, 200, 400 and 800 photons), the median error falls from 0.073 ∘ 0.073^{\circ} to 0.023 ∘ 0.023^{\circ} , with slope − 0.518 -0.518 [ − 0.785 , − 0.308 ] [-0.785,-0.308] (Figure 11 b): precision against a physical reference, at the rate the theory predicts. Complete recovery within 1 ∘ 1^{\circ} reaches 40% at 800 photons. On these thin, isolated spectra the simple geometric methods keep up: a line fit and an angular histogram given the true vertex also reach 41%. The tuned Hessian ridge detector never recovers all four arms within 1 ∘ 1^{\circ} and returns fewer than four arms in 78% of the draws at 800 photons; the fit leads it by 38.3 points [ 25.0 , 51.7 ] [25.0,51.7] at 400 and 800 photons. We used the Porto taxi traces released for the ECML/PKDD 2015 challenge ( Moreira-Matias et al., 2013 ) , kept the fixes of moving vehicles, and took the true geometry of each intersection from OpenStreetMap ( OpenStreetMap contributors, 2026 ) . A site entered only if the maps of 2014 and 2026 agree on it (same number of arms, vertex within 3 m, every arm within 2 ∘ 2^{\circ} ) and every arm runs straight to 40 m. Of 117 sites, the 21 in randomly assigned one-kilometre tiles served for development; the protocol, including the tuned settings of every detector, was frozen before any estimate on the other 96 intersections in 27 tiles. From windows of radius 40 m we drew 25 to 1,600 fixes, three times each. The fit is the earlier implementation of the two-Gaussian model with the count chosen by BIC. Averaged over all sizes, the fit recovers the intersection exactly 14.2 points [ 8.0 , 21.7 ] [8.0,21.7] more often than the tuned Hessian ridge detector, and 35.0 to 46.7 points more often than Steger’s detector, a line fit, an angular histogram and skeletonization (Figure 12 ). The median arm error of fits with the correct count falls with slope − 0.49 -0.49 [ − 0.57 , − 0.42 ] [-0.57,-0.42] from 25 to 400 fixes, while the detector’s levels off at 4.4 ∘ 4.4^{\circ} to 4.7 ∘ 4.7^{\circ} from 400 fixes on. The mixture earns its place here. A one-Gaussian fit absorbs the heavy tail of GPS error with an extra arm: from 200 fixes on it over-counts in 12 to 17% of the windows, against 5 to 9% for two Gaussians, which recover 7.3, 8.7, 5.0 and 8.2 points more intersections at 200, 400, 800 and 1,600 fixes. Per-arm sandwich intervals covered the map directions in only 74 to 84% of cases at 100 to 400 fixes, as map errors of a few metres would produce. The same frozen settings failed every prespecified criterion on 39 intersections in Berlin and Chicago from a public map-construction benchmark ( Ahmed et al., 2015 ) and on 8 in Beijing ( Zheng et al., 2010 ) .

There the Hessian detector led the fit by 19.5 points [ 13.1 , 28.6 ] [13.1,28.6] , and in Beijing the two tied ( − 0.4 -0.4 [ − 13.4 , 11.3 ] [-13.4,11.3] ). Singular and weakly identified models. Parameter estimation in finite mixtures slows down when components merge or vanish ( Ho and Nguyen, 2016 ) , the Laplace approximation behind the BIC can fail at such points ( Drton and Plummer, 2017 ) , and weak identification in semiparametric models has a theory of its own ( Kaji, 2021 ) . Our blur is such a mixture, and it is worse than weakly identified at a balanced crossing: it is not identified at all. The geometry nevertheless keeps the rate n − 1 / 2 n^{-1/2} through every one of these singularities, because the degeneracy lies entirely in the nuisance. Target identifiability under generative indeterminacy ( Xi and Bloem-Reddy, 2023 ) separates what data can determine from what they cannot; we add a uniform Lipschitz bound and a rate for the determined part, and the analytic order criterion of Proposition 4 is a general route to such bounds.

General Lipschitz stability results for inverse problems with finite measurements ( Bourgeois, 2013 ; Alberti and Santacesaria, 2022 ) assume an injective forward map, which fails here. 10 Discussion A blur that cannot be calibrated need not blur the geometry. The mechanism is general: far along an arm the data show the blur only through a centered transverse profile, whose mass and mean return the weight and the line, and a change of direction shifts that profile by an amount that grows with distance. Proposition 4 turns this kind of order comparison into a uniform Lipschitz bound. The same route is open for other targets observed through a nuisance that cannot be identified, such as an edge under an unknown point-spread function or a source position under an unknown beam; in each case the work is an asymptotic argument that shows the target changing no later than the observation. The practical lesson is equally direct. Modeling the blur beats removing it by smoothing, even when the blur itself is lost. On junctions assembled from measured localizations from three laboratories, on natural microtubule junctions, on X-ray grating spectra and on road intersections traced by taxis, the likelihood fit recovers junctions more often than a Hessian ridge detector, at a fixed or a selected scale, or matches the best simple method, and it does not widen acute angles. Measured widefield images show that actual crossings sit at the ambiguity the theory describes, and a blur class with several widths pays off where the error has heavy tails. The results also mark where the approach stops. It needs a candidate window and point data; finding the windows is a detection problem that we do not treat.

It needs data with a density: on raw widefield frames of blinking fluorophores, whose pixels are not independent point positions, the fit over-counts arms and the Hessian detector recovers 18 to 21 points more junctions, and on GPS traces with little road signal and stacked duplicate coordinates it lost to the same detector. The theorems describe a global fit of the model, and the local search we run falls short of it by an amount that we measured rather than bounded. And the rate n − 1 / 2 n^{-1/2} belongs to straight arms: curvature costs a bias set by the curvature at the scale of the blur, which no number of points removes at a fixed blur. Data.
